mappings.note: Bile breaking down fat and neutralising acid: the secretion described by what it does in digestion.
Names the pancreas as the source of pancreatic juice: an organ identified.
Names the small intestine as the main site of absorption: locating the organ, not describing the mechanism.
Names the villi, the finger-like projections of the intestinal lining.
Water and salt absorption as the large intestine's job: a functional step of the process.
Names egestion as the removal of undigested waste.
Names ruminants as the group of cud-chewing animals: organisms placed in a class.
Names rumination as the process of bringing food back to be chewed again. The item naming the animals is on LO-115.
Sets exhaled air against inhaled air on oxygen and carbon dioxide content, which is differentiating two samples of a material by their properties.
The circulatory system as the body's transport network: what that system does, so the process outcome.
Why smoking damages the lungs and raises disease risk: health knowledge that bears on a personal choice, so the day-to-day outcome.
Groups birds, reptiles and land-dwelling adult frogs with mammals as lung breathers: organisms classified by respiratory organ.
Names gills as the organ fish use, an organ identified by its role.
A frog using lungs on land and skin in water: two mechanisms in one animal described, so the process outcome rather than a classification.
Earthworms exchanging gas straight through moist skin: the mechanism described.
Traces air from nostrils through nasal passages and windpipe to the alveoli: the pathway described in prose. Not LO-121, since nothing is drawn.
Ribs and diaphragm acting together to enlarge the chest during inhalation.
The same pair reversing to force air out during exhalation.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide crossing the thin alveolar walls: the exchange step explained.
Lime water turns milky with exhaled air because it carries far more carbon dioxide: the observed difference traced to its cause. Not LO-116, because the experiment is recalled rather than run.
How water over the gills lets dissolved oxygen into the blood: the fish's respiratory mechanism.
The frog's two modes of breathing described at greater length.
The earthworm's skin breathing described at greater length.
The circulatory system linking digestion and respiration by carrying nutrients, oxygen and waste: how the three processes connect.
Why oral hygiene matters and one practice to follow: the learning turned into a daily habit.
The whole journey of food with the process occurring in each organ: the fullest process description in the chapter.

Names carbon dioxide as the waste of the energy-releasing reaction, which is the respiration relation LO-119 names. Not LO-118, because the item asks for a product of the reaction rather than how breathing works.
Whether pulling the sheet models inhalation and why the balloons fill: explaining the working of the constructed model.
Why a cow must ruminate, given fibrous grass and microbial breakdown: the process explained in terms of what it achieves.
An antacid neutralising excess stomach acid to relieve discomfort: dealing with acidity in daily life.
Gas exchange at the alveoli and the transport of both gases in blood: the respiratory process in full.
Human against ruminant digestion, single stomach against rumen and cellulose handling: two kinds of organism differentiated by structure and function, which is what LO-114 covers.
Fish, earthworm and human respiration set against each other by habitat and organ: another organism-level differentiation.
Why fibre belongs in the diet and which foods supply it: the learning applied to everyday eating.
Where carbohydrate, protein and fat digestion each happen: the process traced for all three food groups.
Structure and function of the respiratory system together with the breathing mechanism: the process described end to end.
Breathing against cellular respiration on purpose, site, inputs and outputs: two processes explained side by side, which is LO-118 rather than LO-114, since processes and not organisms are compared.
